theme: Unit 12 review, Hezekiah, Isaiah & the Assyrian Crisis
memoryText: Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!
memoryVerseMeditation:
This is the cry of the seraphim in Isaiah’s vision, and it is the anchor of the whole unit. Everything you have read, from the vineyard song to the suffering Servant to the fall of Nineveh, flows from who God is. He is holy.

“Holy, holy, holy.” Hebrew has no way to say “more” or “most.” Instead it repeats. To say a word three times is to say it as strongly as language can. Only this one attribute of God is ever repeated three times in the Bible. He is utterly set apart, in power, in purity, and in glory. All other things that we call holy are holy because they are connected to him.

“Is the LORD of hosts.” The holy one is not an abstract force. He is the LORD, the covenant God who has a name and who keeps promises. He is also the Lord of hosts, the commander of the armies of heaven. The one who stands against Assyria is the one who reigns over every power.

“The whole earth is full of his glory.” The seraphim see glory in every corner of creation. God’s glory is not limited to the temple. It fills the whole earth. Later in Isaiah, we learn that the knowledge of that glory will cover the earth as the waters cover the sea, and that all flesh will see it together.

Say this verse from memory, and let it shape how you approach God. The holy God has also become your Savior. He sent a seraph with a coal, and, in Christ, he removed your guilt. The one who is holy has made a way for you to stand before him. He calls us to say with the seraphim, and with all creation, “Holy, holy, holy.”
unitRecap: This unit covered one of the most important periods in Old Testament history and one of the greatest books of prophecy. King Hezekiah trusted the LORD when Assyria surrounded Jerusalem, spread Sennacherib’s letter before him, and saw 185,000 soldiers struck down in a night. Isaiah, who prophesied through the crisis, saw the Lord high and lifted up, heard the cry of “Holy, holy, holy,” was cleansed and sent, and announced Immanuel, the child born to us, and the shoot from Jesse’s stump. Chapters 40 to 55 gave comfort to exiles and introduced the Servant, who was despised and rejected, pierced for our transgressions, and yet exalted. You paused on the doctrine of the atonement. Chapters 56 to 66 closed with the invitation to everyone who thirsts, the Spirit-anointed herald, and the promise of new heavens and a new earth. Nahum showed that God’s patience with Nineveh ended, Habakkuk taught that the righteous shall live by faith, and Zephaniah ended with the God who sings over his people.
weekInReview: This week you finished the book of Isaiah and the prophets of the Assyrian crisis. You read about the fast God chooses, the Spirit-anointed one whom Jesus identified as himself, and the great prayer asking God to tear open the heavens. You read God’s answer of a new creation, where the wolf and the lamb feed together and sorrow is no more. You then read three short books: Nahum, which announced the fall of the city that once repented; Habakkuk, who argued with God and learned to live by faith, and who rejoiced in the LORD though everything failed; and Zephaniah, who warned of the Day of the LORD and ended with God exulting over his people with loud singing. The week taught that God is holy and just, that faith is the way to live in uncertain times, and that the God who judges is the God who saves.

reviewQuestions.question: What does Isaiah’s vision of God in chapter 6 teach about worship?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Think about the order of the vision: God’s holiness, Isaiah’s confession, the cleansing coal, and the call to go. What does each step show about how we come before God, and how does the vision change a person?

reviewQuestions.question: Who is the Servant in Isaiah 40-55, and what does he do?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Look at the four Servant Songs (42:1-4, 49:1-6, 50:4-9, 52:13-53:12). Consider his calling, his gentleness, his obedience, and his mission to the nations. How does the New Testament say Jesus fulfills this role (Matthew 12:15-21; Acts 8:32-35)?

reviewQuestions.question: How does Isaiah 53 describe substitutionary atonement?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Notice the repeated words “our” and “his.” Write a few sentences about what the Servant bore, why he bore it, and what the result is for those who trust in him. Compare with Romans 3:21-26 and 1 Peter 2:24.

reviewQuestions.question: What does “the righteous shall live by his faith” mean in Habakkuk’s context?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Recall the dilemma: injustice in Judah, Babylon coming as a rod, and God’s silence. What does it mean to live by faith when the answer is delayed? Consider Habakkuk 3:17-19 and how Paul uses the verse in Romans 1:17.

prayerPrompts: Thank God for the Servant who was pierced for your transgressions.
Thank him for what he has taught you through Isaiah and the prophets.
Ask him to keep the unit verse before you.
